author: NASASpaceflight
description:
NSF coverage of SpaceX's Starship Flight 14. Starship’s first orbital mission is expected to fly at an altitude approximately 275 km above Earth and complete approximately six orbits around the planet over the course of a nearly 10-hour flight, with splashdown targeted in the Pacific Ocean to the west of Chile.
 
The Starship upper stage’s primary objectives include the first orbital insertion maneuver, the deployment of 26 Starlink V3 satellites, a deorbit burn using a single Raptor engine while in space, and a controlled reentry, descent, and splashdown in the Pacific Ocean. Starship will only execute a burn to enter orbit after the flight control team has ensured there is sufficient redundancy on hardware critical to doing the subsequent deorbit burn at the end of the mission.

author: NASASpaceflight
description:
Flight 14 may be days away with the first morning launch window since Flight 5, yet Pad 2 currently holds Ship 42 - assigned to Flight 15 - for chopsticks catch simulations and ship quick-disconnect alignment after cryo testing at Massey’s, while Booster 21 and Ship 41 remain at the production site completing preflight checkouts and FTS installation following their static fire campaigns.

This week’s NSF Starship Update covers Flight 13’s mixed results (successful Ship 40 splashdown and Raptor relight versus Booster 20 landing-burn engine failures), SpaceX’s push for controlled Gulf splashdown and reuse ahead of HLS commitments, new FCC filings for a fully orbital trajectory and Starlink V3, expanded Pacific and Indian Ocean landing zones, Pad 2 landing-rail/deluge/OLM work, Pad 1 tower and chopsticks upgrades, Gigabay crane and enclosure progress, Booster 23 stacking with ice-filter mounts, Starfactory nosecones for Ships 44-46, the proposed Massey’s haul road, LC-39A tank-farm activ
title: SpaceX Just Lifted The WRONG Starship? | Starship Update
